language_wrapper: Consider positive integers n with exactly three proper divisors (positive integral divisors of n excluding n itself). Determine how many such n satisfy all of the following: (1) exactly two of the proper divisors are less than {a}; (2) the remaining proper divisor lies in the interval [{a}, {b}); and (3) the sum of the two larger proper divisors is congruent to {r} modulo {m}. Give your answer as an integer count.
hardness_rationale: The seed problem reduces to classifying integers with exactly three proper divisors (d(n)=4) as either p^3 or pq, and then counting under a simple size constraint. This family strengthens the task by: (1) imposing a two-threshold condition that partitions the three proper divisors across an interval split, forcing careful structural casework between p^3 and pq; and (2) adding an arithmetic progression constraint on the sum of the two larger proper divisors modulo m. The solution now requires classifying the structure, translating the interval conditions precisely, and counting primes (and prime pairs) in ranges with a congruence filter, which is a clear step up in combinatorial and number-theoretic complexity from the seed. The verifier enforces that both structural cases contribute and that the total count is nontrivial, preventing easy shortcuts.
notes: Proof sketch for correctness: If a positive integer n has exactly three proper divisors, then d(n)=4. Hence n is either p^3 or pq with distinct primes p<q. In the p^3 case, the proper divisors are {1,p,p^2}. The condition that exactly two proper divisors are less than a and the remaining one lies in [a,b) forces p<a<=p^2<b; the sum of the two larger proper divisors equals p+p^2, yielding the congruence condition p+p^2≡r (mod m). In the pq case, the proper divisors are {1,p,q}. The condition that exactly two are less than a with one in [a,b) forces p<a<=q<b; the sum of the two larger proper divisors equals p+q, giving p+q≡r (mod m). The two cases are disjoint, and each valid prime (or prime pair) produces a distinct n, proving the counting formula. Implementation details: The generator selects ranges ensuring enough primes to avoid triviality and applies a congruence class filter. The verifier recomputes the counts directly from the definition (primality checks and congruence tests) and rejects instances lacking contributions from both structural cases or with an overall tiny solution set to maintain difficulty.
source_question: How many positive integers have exactly three proper divisors (positive integral divisors excluding itself), each of which is less than 50?
